topic: Linear Transformations and Matrices: The Language of Space
target_audience: Undergraduate students or advanced high school students

sections.title: Prerequisites: Vectors as Coordinates
sections.content: Briefly review that a vector is an arrow in space starting from the origin (0,0), represented by coordinates [x, y]. Introduce the 'basis vectors' i-hat (1,0) and j-hat (0,1) as the building blocks of the 2D plane.
sections.example: Visualize a small robot character standing at the origin of a coordinate grid, with two glowing arrows, i-hat (red) and j-hat (green), pointing along the axes.

sections.title: Defining Linear Transformation Visually
sections.content: Explain that a 'transformation' is a function that takes an input vector and spits out an output vector. For it to be 'linear', two rules must hold: 1) The origin remains fixed. 2) All grid lines must remain parallel and evenly spaced after the movement.
sections.example: Animate a standard square grid warping, stretching, and tilting. Show a 'non-linear' example where the grid lines curve, then 'snap' them back to straight lines to illustrate linearity.

sections.title: The Secret of the Basis Vectors
sections.content: Introduce the core concept: To track how any vector in the entire plane moves, we only need to track where i-hat and j-hat land. If we know the new coordinates of i-hat and j-hat, we can describe the entire transformation.
sections.example: Suppose i-hat moves from (1,0) to (3, -2) and j-hat moves from (0,1) to (2, 1). Every other point on the grid follows their lead proportionately.

sections.title: The Matrix: A Storage Device
sections.content: Explain that a 2x2 matrix is simply a way to package the landing spots of i-hat and j-hat. The first column is where i-hat landed; the second column is where j-hat landed. This matrix represents the entire transformation.
sections.example: Write a matrix where the left column is [3, -2] and the right column is [2, 1]. Use color-coding (red for i-hat's column, green for j-hat's column) to link the numbers to the visual arrows.

sections.title: Calculation: Moving any Vector
sections.content: Demonstrate how to calculate the new position of any vector [x, y] by multiplying it by the matrix. Explain that the new vector is simply 'x' times the new i-hat plus 'y' times the new j-hat.
sections.example: Take a vector v = [1, 2]. To find its new spot, calculate 1*[3, -2] + 2*[2, 1] = [7, 0]. Visualize the vector 'v' jumping to its new position on the warped grid.

sections.title: Application: Character Animation
sections.content: Show how these matrices are used in computer graphics. A 'Scaling' matrix stretches an object, while a 'Rotation' matrix spins it. These are fundamental to how characters are moved in video games.
sections.example: A 2D cat sprite is drawn on the grid. Apply a 'Shear' matrix [[1, 1], [0, 1]]. The cat leans over to the side as the grid tilts, demonstrating the matrix in action for visual effects.
